1. Core Clinical Tension: Acute visual loss and fulminant hypopyon following traumatic corneal injury by a wooden stick classically represents acute bacterial or fungal endophthalmitis. The rapid progression to panophthalmitis despite broad-spectrum antimicrobial coverage masks an unexpected primary ocular mycobacterial infection in a patient without systemic tuberculosis.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint is defined by the emergency ophthalmic presentation and initial ocular ultrasonography, before corneal scrapings, vitreous tap microbiologic analyses, evisceration, and histopathologic/molecular studies.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute post-traumatic bacterial endophthalmitis was the primary working diagnosis, but excluded by negative bacterial smears and lack of response to fortified topical and intravitreal antibiotics; fungal endophthalmitis (often associated with vegetative trauma) was considered, but fungal smears were negative and hourly topical natamycin failed to prevent deterioration. The diagnosis pivots on histopathology of eviscerated ocular tissue revealing caseous granulomatous necrosis with positive acid-fast bacilli staining and PCR confirmation.
case_prompt:
A 46-year-old woman presents to the ophthalmology emergency service with acute, severe right eye pain and sudden diminution of vision, occurring three days after sustaining ocular trauma from a wooden stick. She has no prior history of chronic ocular disease, pulmonary symptoms, or known infectious contacts.

On physical examination, visual acuity in the right eye is reduced to light perception only with inaccurate projection of light rays; visual acuity in the left eye is +0.2 LogMAR. Ocular inspection of the right eye reveals purulent conjunctival discharge with matting of the eyelashes, a sealed corneal perforation accompanied by dense corneal infiltrates, and an anterior chamber completely filled with fibrinous exudate.

Bedside ocular ultrasonography of the right eye demonstrates dense vitreous exudates with an attached retina, consistent with acute endophthalmitis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Traumatic corneal perforation accompanied by rapid hypopyon and severe vitritis pointed strongly to fulminant bacterial endophthalmitis; however, corneal scrapings, conjunctival swabs, and diagnostic vitreous tap were negative for bacteria, and the eye deteriorated despite intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Corneal scrapings and conjunctival swabs sent for bacterial and fungal smears were negative. Diagnostic vitreous tap for bacterial and fungal smears was also done, and intravitreal antibiotics (vancomycin 1 mg in 0.1 ml and ceftazidime 2 mg in 0.1 ml) were administered.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Vegetative ocular injury from a wooden stick commonly introduces filamentous fungi, but fungal smears from corneal scrapings and vitreous tap were negative, and hourly fortified topical natamycin failed to arrest progression to panophthalmitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The vitreous tap was also negative for bacterial and fungal smears. However, the patient developed panophthalmitis in 24 h with positive t-sign and thickened retinochoroid on ultrasonography [Figure 1b] that led to the painful blind eye.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Histopathologic evaluation of eviscerated ocular tissue demonstrated necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis, confirmed by positive acid-fast bacilli staining and PCR detection of mycobacterial antigen in corneal tissue.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Histopathological examination showed the presence of lymphocytic infiltrate with caseous necrosis suggesting granulomatous inflammation [Figure 1c]. Staining for acid-fast bacilli was positive [Figure 1d]. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of the corneal tissue also showed positivity for the tubercular antigen.

editor_comments: Case prompt terminates before microbiology/evisceration; zero pathogen spoilers; exact quotes matched.
